newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia, Belarus in last-minute talks on union pact.
newsitem.headline: Russia, Belarus in last-minute talks on union pact.

text.p: Presidents Boris Yeltsin of Russia and Alexander Lukashenko of Belarus held last-minute talks on Wednesday about a Union Treaty they were due to sign later in the day, the Kremlin said.
The unscheduled meeting clearly reflected an 11th hour row among Russia's political elite over the scope of the accord, which is intended to tighten ties between the two former Soviet republics.
Most major politicians agree over the need for a closer union but liberals have expressed concern over the secretive way the accord had been prepared and about its contents.
A Kremlin press statement said the two leaders met at 9 a.m. (0500 GMT) for one-on-one talks about the treaty.
Their meeting had been originally scheduled for 11 a.m., to be followed by a signing ceremony at around noon.

Lukashenko, whose crackdown on opponents and distaste for free market economics have drawn criticism from Russia and the West, flew to Moscow late on Tuesday after lengthy talks with Yeltsin aide Ivan Rybkin.
Security Council secretary Rybkin had been sent to Minsk with what the Kremlin called minor amendments to a draft treaty agreed by Lukashenko and Russian officials last month.
But Russia's commercial NTV television, which has openly voiced the concerns of Kremlin liberals, quoted sources close to Lukashenko as saying Yeltsin wanted to scale back the treaty.
"Alexander Lukashenko's reaction was highly explosive," NTV's Minsk correspondent said, forecasting that accords between Belarus and Russia were on the point of collapse.
But Interfax news agency, seen as close to Lukashenko, later quoted an official in his administration as saying the Belarussian leader approved Moscow's "remarks and proposals".
"These corrections do not change the essence of the union treaty nor its scope," the Belarus official said.

A draft of the "Treaty on a Union of Belarus and Russia", obtained by Reuters on Monday, provided for the two former Soviet republics to coordinate foreign, economic and defence policies but stopped short of a merger into a single state.
Yeltsin publicly backed the treaty on Tuesday and Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin insisted it would be signed.

Kremlin sources told Reuters that the details were still in doubt as Yeltsin faced competing claims from supporters and opponents of the union, which aims to build on a bilateral "community" treaty signed exactly a year ago on April 2, 1996.
That deal was signed with great pomp in the Kremlin and blessed by Russian Orthodox Patriarch Alexiy II. This time, media access is being limited.

The opposition has been behind the scenes, partly because the idea of union with their 10 million Slav cousins is broadly popular with the 150 million Russians. A poll by the "Public Opinion" foundation on Tuesday found 59 percent wanted a merger.

Liberals, in a strong position since Anatoly Chubais was named first deputy to Chernomyrdin last month, fear union could harm Russia's economy and make Lukashenko, who once professed an admiration for Adolf Hitler, a key player in Moscow politics.

Aman Tuleyev, a communist brought in last year as minister for relations with former Soviet states, said the liberals had managed to water down the plans and Yeltsin and Lukashenko would now sign only a 10-point "memorandum", allowing further public debate about a detailed treaty.
